title: Combinatorial lines and a lipogram
line: Write interchangeable lines, then measure what survives a forbidden letter.
thesis: Write one event as a family of texts. Every legal assembly should preserve the incident and leave room for a distinct voice. Use the missing letter to discover which facts are hardest to name.
state: ◻(Slot) has a position, event ID, grammar, and three candidate lines. ◻(Combination) has one line ID per slot. [assemble] yields a text. [exclude letter] restricts the admissible IDs in each slot.
invariant: Keep event order and outcomes fixed. Write six slots with three distinct lines per slot. Any line must fit its slot beside every other slot’s choices. Freeze the line bank before applying the secondary lipogram.
concurrency: Agree on tense, viewpoint, and event vocabulary before assigning lines. Different slots can be drafted in parallel. Check cross-slot pronouns and references on the combined bank before freezing it.
swarm: Assign a form designer to the slot contracts, writers to line banks, and a checker to enumeration and character tests. Ask a reader to compare two combinations against the same fact ledger.
proof: Make a six-line incident with three alternatives per line and show two sharply different assemblies. Apply a declared letter ban to the frozen bank and show two surviving texts. Report 3⁶ = 729 possible ID combinations before filtering and the actual survivor count afterward.
fixture: Use the letter E, case-insensitive and with accents folded. Count the product of surviving choices per slot and verify it by enumeration. Aim for at least one survivor in every slot and two choices in one slot. In a negative test, add an É to a candidate and check that it is excluded.
critic: Read the samples without their IDs. Check that each delivers the same six facts and has a recognizable voice. Verify the character rule on the assembled text and inspect the slot with the fewest alternatives.
inquiry: If a line only makes sense beside one specific neighbor, locate the unstated dependency and revise the bank or declare and count an explicit compatibility restriction.
branch: Test a second letter ban against the same frozen bank. If it empties a slot, report which event loses all its available wording.
deliver: Deliver the line bank, a selector or enumeration script, two readable outputs from each mode, and the acceptance counts.
shared: Give E01 through E06 one line each. For the lipogram, try a brass bit cut to fit a lock for E04 and a plank for sitting for E05, then test whether the objects still read clearly.
sources: Describes Queneau’s position-by-position selection among ten sonnet lines.
Defines the forbidden-letter constraint and identifies Perec’s La Disparition.

title: One solution, two clue orders
byline: Ouvroir de littérature policière potentielle · Detective fiction
line: Permute the evidence in a locked-room mystery and count the explanations still possible.
thesis: Let clue order guide suspicion while the same evidence determines the answer. A fair mystery rewards a reader who tracks which account each observation rules out.
state: ◻(Hypothesis) pairs a suspect with an access method. ◻(Clue) cites an observable fact and has a truth value under every hypothesis. ◻(Reveal) orders clue IDs. [intersect] gives the candidates still compatible with the revealed evidence.
invariant: Freeze the room rules, culprit, method, evidence wording, and final clue. Every scheduled clue is true of the solution. Two readings use the same evidence and differ in the order of the earlier clues.
concurrency: Freeze the solution and clue truth table first. Authors can arrange independent reveal orders against that table. Changes to access rules, alibis, or evidence meaning require retesting every order.
swarm: Let a puzzle designer build the room and hypothesis matrix, a scene writer stage observations, and a solver attempt every surviving explanation without reading the answer.
proof: Write two short versions of a sealed-room or sealed-container puzzle. Show the reader where they can pause and solve it before opening the answer. Publish the surviving-set trace after each clue in each version.
fixture: Start with A, B, and C and two methods per suspect. One early clue rules out method 2 and one rules out C. Reveal these in either order, leaving A and B using method 1. The last clue must exclude B through an observable detail available to the reader.
critic: Check that the two openings create different plausible suspicions, the final answer follows from shown facts, and a second valid answer or unstated access route would fail the proof.
inquiry: If readers solve it early, distinguish a deductive leak from a strong guess by asking for the exact disqualifying evidence. Revise the reveal or the clue predicate that caused the leak.
branch: Run a withheld-clue edition and enumerate its remaining solutions. Use the ambiguity to expose what work the final clue actually does.
deliver: Deliver both mystery texts, the room diagram or access ledger, the clue matrix, and a separate solution with the surviving-set traces.
shared: Use the closed service door as a constraint on who could have placed the brass key inside the envelope before E03. Keep the visitor’s later actions and the public station record fixed.
sources: Records Le Lionnais’s classification project on detective-novel structures and the group’s work on enigmas.

title: Fibonacci montage
line: Cut the same six shots twice under an exact frame-count score.
thesis: Give editorial attention a measurable price in frames. Reassign who gets the longest look by changing where a shot sits in the edit.
state: ◻(Shot) has a source ID, first frame, usable range, and an action anchor. ◻(Cut) is a permutation of six IDs. [score position] assigns an exact output duration and [trim] takes that many contiguous source frames.
invariant: Use one frozen inventory of six shots, each exactly once per edit. Positions take 8, 13, 21, 34, 55, and 89 frames at 24 fps. Use straight cuts and a fixed in-point with 89 usable frames per shot. Keep the same ambience bed and any short sync cues attached to their source shots.
concurrency: Freeze the footage, anchor in-points, sound policy, and duration score before editors branch. Each editor owns a permutation. Any trim-source or sync change invalidates both edit lists.
swarm: Have one crew stage and lock the six shots, two editors choose their openings and endings, and an export checker count decoded frames and match them to the source manifest.
proof: Make a chronological cut and a second version that opens on a consequence. Export both in constant frame rate with edit lists showing source ranges and cumulative output frames. Each shot needs an action cue legible even in its shortest assigned window.
fixture: Use E01–E06 for the first order and E05, E01, E02, E03, E04, E06 for the second. Both exports contain exactly 220 frames. Intentionally export one 221-frame version to verify that the duration check catches a one-frame tail.
critic: Screen both cuts before looking at the edit lists. Mark where you first infer why the key sits on the bench. Check that every action ID remains legible and the final service-door state survives the trim.
inquiry: If the shortest shot loses its action, test whether the cue begins too late or its composition requires a longer look. Adjust the source staging before freezing a new pair.
branch: Double every term if the longer duration earns its own version. Show what a uniform increase changes with the same orders and source anchors.
deliver: Deliver two playable cuts, the footage manifest, the edit decisions, and the decoded-frame counts.
shared: Start the second cut with the key landing on the bench, then show how it got there. Give the closing shot room to establish that the door stays shut.
sources: Gazette Drouot · La Machine à tuer le temps dossier
Documents a collective Oucipo script, a 42-shot photographic notebook, and three variations. Fibonacci durations are the rule of this SCION exercise.

title: Tile permutation and a forbidden hue
line: Change the composition by moving the same painted tiles across a grid.
thesis: Make adjacency create a figure that the individual tiles cannot supply. Reassemble the same inventory so a continuous form becomes a dispersed field.
state: ◻(Tile) has an ID, orientation, pigments, and motif mask. ◻(Canvas) is a bijection between sixteen tiles and a four-by-four grid. [permute] changes site assignments. [measure] finds orthogonally adjacent motif components.
invariant: Freeze sixteen equal tiles and their orientations. Declare one excluded hue group and the admissible swatches before painting. Every assembly displays each tile exactly once and keeps its pigments, marks, and orientation fixed.
concurrency: Assign tile painters after freezing shared swatches and motif-edge conventions. Two layout makers can work against the finished tile inventory. Changing any tile forces a new inventory and a new comparison.
swarm: Assign a palette keeper, tile makers, a layout designer for each assembly, and a critic who sees both canvases at equal size and distance.
proof: Arrange six marked tiles into one connected figure in assembly A. In assembly B disperse the same six so every connected component has at most two tiles. Show both canvases side by side and keep a photograph or source layer for every tile.
fixture: Use six amber-marked tiles and ten unmarked tiles with a palette that excludes blue. In rows 1–2 and columns 1–3 the six form one component. Pairs on r1c1–r1c2, r3c1–r3c2, and r4c3–r4c4 form three separate components.
critic: Inspect the frozen swatches and both tile manifests. Identify whether a viewer can trace the continuous motif in A and where the figure dissolves in B.
inquiry: If the connected cluster looks fragmented, compare the declared adjacency with actual motif contact at the seams. Revise the tile edges or record the difference between grid and visual connectivity.
branch: Build a separate inventory permitting tile rotations and retest the same grid coordinates. Measure whether rotating marks changes the perceived figure while the occupancy graph stays fixed.
deliver: Deliver two panels, an indexed tile sheet, the swatch list, and the component counts for both layouts.
shared: Translate the closed door, key, and bench into paintable motifs. Let the brass color tie the fragments into a key shape in one arrangement and scatter it through the station in the other.
sources: Identifies the workshop for potential painting and gives an official point of entry to its work.
Catalogues Thieri Foulc’s accounts of potential painting and Oupeinpo publications.

title: Grammatical mold, donor lexicon
byline: Atelier de littérature assistée par la mathématique et les ordinateurs · Paul Braffort and Jacques Roubaud
line: Build a runnable generator that puts one text’s vocabulary into another text’s grammar.
thesis: Make the mold and the dictionary independently inspectable so a reader can tell which text supplies the sentence shape and which supplies its verbal material.
state: ◻(Mold) alternates fixed text with typed slots. ◻(Lexeme) has a donor location, lemma, part of speech, inflections, and optional prosody. [solve with seed] selects a compatible filling and logs every choice.
invariant: Freeze the source mold, donor spans, slot types, and declared agreement rules. Preserve fixed words and punctuation. Every inserted lemma must come from the donor and every surface form must have a documented inflection. Report an unfillable slot explicitly.
concurrency: Source parsing and donor annotation can proceed independently against a shared tag schema. Freeze both before generator runs. Record the data revisions and seed for every sample.
swarm: Split mold extraction, donor lexicon building, selection and inflection, and read-back verification. Let the linguist resolve dependencies before the programmer treats the slots as independent.
proof: From an original source of two to four lines, remove content words at four or more typed positions. Build a tiny runnable generator and a closed, attributable donor lexicon. Return two distinct legal outputs, their fill traces, and a run that reproduces one output from its seed.
fixture: Use a mold with a singular noun that agrees with a present-tense verb, plus at least one adjective slot. Run three recorded seeds. Remove every compatible verb from the donor in a negative run and name the blocked slot in the failure report.
critic: Reconstruct each output from the mold and the trace. Check agreement, position, donor provenance, and any meter actually declared. Read both outputs and identify which change the new vocabulary makes audible.
inquiry: When the corpus cannot fill the mold, identify whether part of speech, agreement, or prosody exhausts the candidate pool. Test one documented change at a time.
branch: Swap the donor corpus while holding the mold and rules fixed. A separate relaxed run may drop one declared constraint and must identify the rule it dropped.
deliver: Deliver the source texts, typed mold, annotated lexicon, runnable generator with invocation, outputs, and slot-level traces.
shared: Keep the grammar of a short report of E01–E06. Fill it from an original list of nautical or astronomical words and trace any changes to the apparent setting.
sources: Paul Braffort · ALAMO, une expérience de douze ans
Describes removing Rimbaud’s content words and applying a Baudelaire lexicon under prosodic, syntactic, and semantic constraints.
Catalogues ALAMO’s generator and describes its mold-and-lexicon method.

title: A palindromic tasting menu
line: Mirror five cooking techniques around one course and leave an ingredient family out.
thesis: Let a technique recur with a different role in the meal. The last course should give the first a recognizable echo through texture or aroma.
state: ◻(Course) has a position, defining technique, sensory role, and ingredient tree. ◻(Menu) is an ordered course list. [mirror] pairs positions i and 6−i and [expand] resolves ingredients inside stocks, sauces, and garnishes.
invariant: Use five courses with technique sequence roast, steam, poach, steam, roast. Choose an excluded ingredient family up front. Apply it to all nested ingredients. Keep position pairs distinct as dishes while sharing the declared technique.
concurrency: Draft mirrored pairs against the same exclusion ledger. Assign one owner to verify all subrecipes and another to check equipment and service timing across courses.
swarm: Have cooks design the paired courses and the hinge. Give the prep planner the actual quantities and equipment. Have a critic review the menu and any available tasting evidence against the declared progression.
proof: Make a five-course menu with recipe cards, defining steps, an ingredient substitution ledger, and a common prep timeline. Make the center course change the direction of the sequence from opening to closing.
fixture: Exclude onion, garlic, leek, shallot, chive, and scallion for the exercise. Walk every sauce and stock to its base ingredients. Seed one stock containing onion to test rejection. Mark any opaque purchased ingredient as unverified.
critic: Check execution order, technique symmetry, and the full ingredient tree. Describe what the design predicts and record sensory judgments only for food actually tasted.
inquiry: If the mirrored courses feel redundant, keep the technique and change one sensory axis such as temperature, texture, or the ingredient carrying the shared aroma.
branch: Make a second menu with the same technique score and exclusion using a different seasonal inventory. Track which substitutions preserve the mirrored relationships.
deliver: Deliver the menu, recipe and prep cards, the expanded ingredient list, and a brief account of the hinge and mirrored pairs.
shared: Use the station’s opening, arrival, and departure as structural cues. Put a single revealing course in the center and echo the outer courses by technique.
sources: Names Oucuipo as the workshop for potential cuisine.
Régine Detambel · Abrégé de littérature potentielle
Identifies Noël Arnaud’s role in Oucuipo and introduces his writing on culinary theory.

title: A reversible stage score
line: Perform one cue score forward and back with an explicit inverse for each action.
thesis: Use the same score to make an arrival and an extraction. Give the reverse passage enough dramatic intent that an audience can follow what each performer wants.
state: ◻(StageState) tracks performer marks, prop locations, and resettable cues. ◻(Card) has a line or silence, a forward action, an inverse, and both preconditions. [play] applies a card in the declared direction and advances the state.
invariant: Freeze six cue cards, their words, and each inverse before rehearsal. Forward order is 1 through 6. Reverse order is 6 through 1 and starts in the actual forward ending state. Track reversibility in the recorded prop, position, and cue states.
concurrency: Only one owner changes a shared transition in the cue table. Blocking and line delivery can be explored independently after the table is frozen. Rehearse the full chain once before judging either direction.
swarm: Have a score writer define each state change, performers block both branches, and a stage manager log placements and successful undo. Let a spectator report roles and stakes from both runs.
proof: Run the six-card score forward and immediately in reverse. Publish the script and before/after state at every cue. Use an envelope with a resettable closure and a reversible light or bell indicator if those props change.
fixture: A visitor crosses a mark, turns on a cue, opens a flap, removes a key, places it on a bench, and leaves. Require the reverse run to return each object and performer to its initial tracked state. Try one inverse from the wrong prop position and check that it fails.
critic: Trace props and marks without a reset between passages. Ask a spectator to describe each passage’s objective and report the earliest cue that loses dramatic or physical continuity.
inquiry: When a card consumes or irreversibly alters a prop, replace it with a resettable stage action and retest both directions.
branch: Exchange performers at the midpoint in a separate run. Freeze character commitments and transfer the role and held prop together under a declared handoff.
deliver: Deliver both readable cue orders, the prop-state ledger, and a rehearsal recording or a timed staging plan with its verification status.
shared: Play E01–E06 straight, then stage the visitor’s return through the reverse chain. Keep the service door closed in both passages.
sources: Identifies the workshop for potential theatre.
Dates Stanley Chapman’s London workshop to 1991 and lists its theatre publications.

title: One image, two orders of captions
byline: Ouvroir de bande dessinée potentielle · Comics
line: Repeat one drawing nine times and let two traversal orders change what its captions mean.
thesis: Give the eye one stable image and the reader two changing contexts. A line at the center should acquire a different referent or intention according to which captions led to it.
state: ◻(Cell) has a coordinate, shared art ID, and immutable lettering. ◻(Route) is an ordered set of nine cell IDs. [read] accumulates a path-local sequence of claims and referents.
invariant: Use one drawing at the same crop and scale in every cell. Freeze one caption per cell. Readers traverse the same 3×3 page across rows or down columns. Both routes share their first and last cell. Route labels live outside the panels.
concurrency: Freeze the plate first. Use one lettering editor for both routes because every caption affects both readings. Compare both readings on each candidate edit.
swarm: Have an artist draw the plate, a letterer write captions against both routes, and two readers each reconstruct one path before exchanging their accounts.
proof: Make one nine-panel page and two annotated route transcripts. Give one reading a straightforward report and the other a plausible account of intent. Use the central caption as the hinge and let the shared end close both accounts.
fixture: Row order is 11, 12, 13, 21, 22, 23, 31, 32, 33. Column order is 11, 21, 31, 12, 22, 32, 13, 23, 33. Cell 22 follows 21 in the first reading and 12 in the second. Let its caption point to a different established referent in each.
critic: Verify plate identity and caption stability across routes. Ask readers to point to the earlier captions that license their different readings of cell 22.
inquiry: If the accounts only differ in order, revise the hinge or its immediate lead-ins, then check whether both routes still have an intelligible ending.
branch: Produce an enlarged accessible reading of each route with the same art and lettering. Check that reading linearized text still preserves the hinge, and record visual ambiguities that depend on the grid.
deliver: Deliver the page, the plate and lettering layers, both route diagrams or lists, and the independent readings.
shared: Repeat a wide plate of the station bench beneath the closed door. Use the lettering to give one route the incident and the other the suspicion that the key was deliberately left.
sources: Cité internationale de la bande dessinée et de l’image · Oubapo
Describes iconic iteration and multiple viable routes through a set of panels.
Identifies Matt Madden’s ninety-nine comic-page variations on one event and their lineage in Queneau.

title: Change one event in the record
line: Fork a dated record at one intervention and trace the consequences.
thesis: Make a counterfactual expose how much an explanation depends on one event. Retain the archival record as a visible baseline and show the chain each conjecture depends on.
state: ◻(Evidence) cites a dated source and proposition. ◻(BaselineEvent) has a time, evidence IDs, and dependencies. [intervene] changes one designated premise. [propagate] adds hypothetical consequences with a named dependency and rationale.
invariant: Keep the source ledger intact and behaviors before the fork fixed. Edit exactly one baseline premise at the fork. Keep independent background facts fixed in both timelines. Mark each downstream claim as attested, hypothetical, or unresolved.
concurrency: Freeze the evidence ledger before historians construct branches. Each branch owns its hypotheticals. Resolve conflicting evidence in the ledger and rerun affected branches when a source changes the baseline.
swarm: Assign an archivist to source provenance, a historian to the intervention and dependency graph, and a skeptic to look for unsupported links and alternative explanations.
proof: Make two parallel timelines with five to seven entries each. Show a shared prefix, one mapped change, and at least two downstream steps. Give each divergence a causal predecessor and state what would weaken the inference.
fixture: In the fictional station record delay the bell by one minute. Freeze the arrival, objects, and closed door. Give a reason for any changed opening or departure time and show the alternative if the visitor would have acted independently of the bell.
critic: Point to the single intervention and reconstruct the proposed chain. Flag silent edits to the baseline and hypothetical inferences presented as sourced evidence.
inquiry: If a consequence follows only under an untested assumption, run the same intervention under its plausible alternative and mark the disagreement.
branch: Make a separate N+7 experiment on a short document. Publish the dictionary version, each original noun, its shifted lemma, and the rule for missing entries. Treat that result as a labeled transformation of the document.
deliver: Deliver the source ledger, both timelines, a dependency map, and the most consequential unresolved assumption.
shared: Use the unchanged station record as the baseline and annotate which deductions about the key depend on the bell’s timing.
sources: Lists the group’s Exercices d’histoire potentielle in a 1995 issue of Monitoires du Cymbalum Pataphysicum.
Credits the Ouhispo with the history contribution to La Réunion.
Describes the dictionary-based noun-substitution rule behind the optional textual branch.

title: A route sampled by the clock
line: Make a contact sheet whose exposures follow a fixed interval and route.
thesis: Let a clock decide which parts of a place earn a frame. Use blanks, rhythms, and repetitions to show what the walk and camera happened to encounter.
state: ◻(Route) has a start, direction, and finish. ◻(Tick) has a scheduled offset, actual capture time, and route position. [expose] records one frame or a missed slot. [contact sheet] preserves the schedule as reading order.
invariant: Declare the route, framing policy, six capture times, and tolerance before departure. Take at most one exposure per scheduled time and keep it in its slot. Keep misses visible and record permitted exposure adjustments.
concurrency: A route planner and contact-sheet designer can prepare independently from the declared schedule. During capture one operator owns each slot. Assemble from the immutable capture log.
swarm: Have a route planner set the sampling rule, a photographer execute it, and an editor lay out the log without choosing preferred frames. Let a reader review the sequence before seeing the map.
proof: Walk one declared segment and build a six-slot contact sheet. Label actual capture time and offset for each frame or a reason for a miss. Include a small route map with the scheduled positions or the actual positions when known.
fixture: Schedule offsets 0, 60, 120, 180, 240, and 300 seconds with a two-second tolerance. Simulate a missed 120-second exposure and keep the third position blank. A frame logged at 125 seconds must fail that slot’s timing check.
critic: Audit the sequence against capture times and route. Ask what the imposed timing revealed or skipped. Point to each miss and any plausible correction that would alter the rule.
inquiry: If the frames cannot show a change across the route, isolate cadence, path, and framing in three candidate explanations and change only the leading one on a new run.
branch: Run the same clock on the reverse route or in a separate overlay experiment pair frames equidistant from the midpoint. Preserve the original six slots in either case.
deliver: Deliver the contact sheet, original frames, route diagram, and exposure log.
shared: Walk the station from entrance to the closed service door. Keep the scheduled third exposure even when the envelope or key sits outside the composition.
sources: Names the founding group and links its classification of photographic constraints.

title: Music that survives a shuffle
line: Compose four modules and verify every possible join in a shuffled piece.
thesis: Give the listener a continuous pulse when sections change places. Let the same modules make different arcs through register, density, or timbre.
state: ◻(Module) has an ID, bar count, tempo, harmonic map, and entry and exit signatures. [join] puts two rendered modules on one beat grid. ◻(Order) uses every ID exactly once.
invariant: Freeze four original four-bar modules in one meter, tempo, and boundary harmony. All directed joins between distinct modules must pass the same pulse, harmonic, and audible seam checks. Use identical module renders in both assemblies.
concurrency: Agree on the joint score and export timing before composers work independently. Test every incoming and outgoing adjacency after a module changes.
swarm: Assign an arranger to boundary conditions, composers to module interiors, and a mixer to seams and rendering. Ask a second listener to judge complete orders before individual joins.
proof: Render two audibly distinct orders and a review reel of the twelve directed joins. Include the closing join for each piece if it is presented as a loop. Explain how the same shared motif functions differently in each order.
fixture: Use modules A, B, C, and D at 100 bpm in 4/4 with a shared D minor boundary. A–B–C–D and C–A–D–B each have sixteen bars. A one-beat insert at an internal transition must fail the beat-grid check.
critic: Listen for dropped beats, harmonic ruptures, cut tails, and indistinct arcs. Verify the full join matrix and mark any seam that needs a new mix or composition.
inquiry: When a join fails, test pulse, pitch, and tail continuity one at a time against the same two renders.
branch: Define two types of musical boundaries and restrict the shuffle to compatible orders. Enumerate the reduced set and compare the audible dynamics with the unrestricted score.
deliver: Deliver the four modules, two complete audio renders, a join-review reel, the score or session, and the test matrix.
shared: Use four modules keyed to arrival, bell, discovery, and exit, with an original bell pulse as the common motif. Compare what the opening tells the listener to expect.
sources: Identifies potential-music workshops in the Ouxpo network.
Documents album constraints including a returning theme and matching beginning and end. All-pairs shuffle compatibility is the rule of this SCION exercise.

title: Runnable code with an acrostic
line: Make one program pass a behavior test and a separate test of its source form.
thesis: Give source code two readers. The interpreter receives useful behavior and the human reader can find a message in the names of the functions that perform it.
state: ◻(Program) has a language, revision, I/O contract, and execution trace. ◻(Form) gives a syntax-tree selector and target string. [run] tests behavior. [read source] extracts the target letters from declarations.
invariant: Freeze the input and output contract before writing. Write six top-level Python function declarations in source order. Their initials must spell a six-letter word. Every function must run on the normal entry path and perform a declared part of the behavior.
concurrency: A behavior checker and a form checker can write their assertions independently. A single integrator owns source edits because changing a declaration can affect both.
swarm: Assign a programmer to the artifact, a test writer to behavior and invocation, and a reader to parse the source order and inspect contribution to the entry path.
proof: Deliver one Python program and checks that run it, exercise all six functions, and extract the initials from top-level function declarations with the standard AST parser. Record independent pass or fail results for output and form.
fixture: Read an input station record and return its six normalized events in order. Use step_in, echo, access_envelope, locate_key, entrust_bench, and depart so the declarations spell SEALED. Swap two declarations with different initials to fail form alone. Alter an emitted event to fail behavior alone.
critic: Run the program from its declared invocation. Check both negative cases and trace every function to a necessary result. Read the source as an acrostic and as maintainable code.
inquiry: If the desired letters force misleading names or empty wrappers, revise the decomposition or choose a different word and freeze a new test fixture.
branch: Build a second compliant implementation under the same behavior contract using a different formal target. Compare where the source form changed the decomposition.
deliver: Deliver the source, input and expected output, runnable check command, and reports for both tests and both negative cases.
shared: Use one function to normalize each of E01–E06. Check the event order and final location of the key in output from the actual entry point.
sources: Lists informatique among the potential workshop domains. The executable acrostic is this SCION exercise.

title: An acrostic made with line breaks
byline: Potential typography · Typographic and visual poetry
line: Keep a text verbatim and use line breaks to reveal a second reading.
thesis: Make the eye discover a short second message before or after it reads the full text. Let lineation carry the difference between the two readings.
state: ◻(Text) holds an ordered token sequence. ◻(Specimen) declares width, font, and allowed typographic operations. [lineate] maps tokens to rows. [read initials] spells a second message from the start of each designed line.
invariant: Use exactly the same characters after normalizing whitespace, in the same order, for both specimens. Lock font family, size, and line height. Allow line breaks, alignment, spacing, and weight.
concurrency: Freeze the text before setting layouts. A typographer can design the comparison while a reader prepares the text-equivalence and line-initial checks.
swarm: Have a writer compose the shared text, a typographer set the two readings, and a reader test the visual and plain-text paths at intended sizes.
proof: Deliver a run-in specimen and a lineated specimen in which three or more line initials form a readable word. Make the second message enrich the original text. Include a print specimen or a responsive preview that preserves line beginnings in its supported widths.
fixture: Use “Keys wait here. Every visitor hears a bell. You will find the door closed.” Break before Every and You to expose K–E–Y. Compare copied text from the two views and test the designed line starts at desktop and 360-pixel widths.
critic: Read at the intended distance and identify the primary text and the acrostic. Flag any forced line wrap, clipping, changed text, or secondary reading that requires a legend to notice.
inquiry: If the secondary reading overwhelms the text, vary initial weight or horizontal spacing one step at a time and test reading order again.
branch: Find a second meaningful acrostic in a longer frozen text by solving for alternate line breaks. Preserve the first specimen for comparison.
deliver: Deliver the original text, two specimens, the line-break map, and text-equivalence and width checks.
shared: Derive a short station notice from E01–E06. Use a second reading to call the eye back to the hidden object.
sources: Lists an Outypopo in its chronology of workshops.
A contemporary group describes working under constraint across poetry, typography, and visual form.

title: Rooms on a knight’s tour
line: Distinguish an admissible sequence of rooms from a route that can actually be walked.
thesis: Let a formal itinerary reorder how a visitor encounters a building. Test what the geometry and the room program do to a tour that works on a board.
state: ◻(Room) has a grid address, program, footprint, and threshold. ◻(Tour) is an ordered room list. [knight move] permits grid offsets (1, 2) or (2, 1) in either direction. [trace] maps each transition to a drawn path.
invariant: Visit each room exactly once from entrance to exit. Every consecutive pair makes a legal knight move on room centers. Draw continuous routes that cross only the intended room thresholds in order. Declare any levels and corridor junctions.
concurrency: Fix the room schedule and endpoints before the tour solver and plan designer branch. A change to any room address, threshold, or programmed stop requires rechecking both graph and plan.
swarm: Have a solver enumerate valid tours, a designer fit one to the room program, and a reviewer trace the path at the scale of the plan.
proof: Produce a twelve-room diagram and a schematic plan. Annotate the walk through all thresholds and mark path crossings and optional choices. Report graph feasibility and drawn walking continuity separately.
fixture: Use a 3×4 grid with entrance r1c1 and exit r3c4. A valid address sequence is 11, 23, 31, 12, 24, 32, 13, 21, 33, 14, 22, 34. Check eleven legal moves independently and show an intentional illegal move or repeated room as a failing case.
critic: Trace the drawn route without jumping across walls or accidentally entering a future room. Check where the visual or physical experience supports the chosen program sequence.
inquiry: If a graph-valid tour has blocked thresholds, identify the geometry that breaks it and test another valid tour or a new documented corridor arrangement.
branch: Keep the plan and reverse a legal tour. Test whether the room program can perform the reverse sequence, with the relationships that depend on the original direction made explicit.
deliver: Deliver the room schedule, tour ledger, schematic plan, traced route, and graph and plan checks.
shared: Assign envelope, bell, key, bench, and service threshold to stops on the tour. Use the remaining rooms to control approach and departure.
sources: Credits Ouarchpo with the model in the 2005 collective project. The knight’s tour is the rule of this SCION exercise.
Identifies architecture as the workshop’s domain.

title: Five primitives, two poster hierarchies
line: Move the same copy and geometric vocabulary into two different reading orders.
thesis: Use placement and scale to change which part of the same message reaches a passerby first. Give the five shapes visual jobs a reader can recognize.
state: ◻(Primitive) has a declared geometry type and allowable parameters. ◻(Poster) places labeled, locked copy blocks and shape instances on a fixed grid. [compose] changes scale, placement, repetition, and depth.
invariant: Lock the copy, background, palette, font family, weights, and page grid. Use circle, rectangle, triangle, line, and arc as the entire drawn vocabulary apart from fixed text. Each composition must use all five and keep text legible.
concurrency: Define the shape primitives and copy before designers branch. Run the same shape and reading checks on both layouts. Share changes to a primitive only by revising the common brief.
swarm: Assign an art director to vocabulary, two layout designers to alternative hierarchies, and a critic to a short timed read at the same scale.
proof: Make two posters from identical words. Give each a different intended first-read block. Ship editable source and rendered previews, with a legend listing every primitive and its placements.
fixture: Set three copy blocks on a 12×18 grid reading “STATION”, “KEY ON BENCH”, and “SERVICE DOOR CLOSED”. Poster A should give the key notice first attention. Poster B should give it to the closed-door notice. Show a primitive audit and compare timed first reads.
critic: Before viewing the placements, record the first block you noticed and the action you inferred. Check the shape inventory and inspect legibility at a small viewing scale.
inquiry: If first reads are the same, change position, size, or surrounding space on a single target in a new iteration and retest.
branch: Map each candidate to a narrow public display using the same copy and primitive vocabulary. Check whether the intended reading hierarchy survives the move.
deliver: Deliver editable posters, rendered previews, the primitive and copy inventories, and the timed reading results.
shared: Turn the station’s bench, brass key, and shut door into a single recurring mark system. Keep the notice verbatim in both designs.
sources: Records an Ougrapo entry among the workshops.
University of Technology Sydney · Open Research
Identifies Ougrapo with graphic design. The five-primitive grammar is the rule of this SCION exercise.

title: Rotate the agenda
line: Hold preferences fixed and see which proposals pass when the agenda starts elsewhere.
thesis: Make procedural power visible by varying the order in which a body can hear proposals. Show how a time limit changes which votes can occur.
state: ◻(Session) has members, fixed ballots, proposal IDs, and allotted slots. [schedule] orders eligible proposals. [truncate] selects the scheduled slots. [tally] calculates adopted proposals from the same ballots and threshold.
invariant: Hold proposals, participants, ballots, eligibility, admission time, and decision threshold fixed. Each proposal consumes one equal slot. Compare a fixed queue and a cyclic agenda with only the starting position changed.
concurrency: Freeze the vote ledger before running agendas. Simulators can process different start positions independently. Keep any strategic response in a separately versioned run.
swarm: Have a facilitator define the procedural rule, a recorder verify vote and time inputs, and a reviewer replay the sessions from the public trace.
proof: Simulate four proposals, four voters, and three slots per session. Print both agendas, the order heard, votes cast, resulting decisions, and deferred proposals. Run all four start positions and count who reaches the agenda.
fixture: Fix yes totals A=4, B=3, C=2, D=4 and a three-vote threshold. A, B, C yields adopted A and B. D, A, B yields adopted D, A, and B. In a full rotation each proposal is heard in three sessions.
critic: Recalculate the outcomes from the disclosed rule. Distinguish ballot support, access to a vote, and adoption. Identify which dependencies would change if participants changed their strategy.
inquiry: If the agendas look equivalent, test whether they admit the same candidates or whether excluded candidates could never pass. Show each surviving causal path.
branch: Run a strategic variant only after the frozen-ballot comparison. Declare whose vote or proposed timing can change and show the effect on the same outcome table.
deliver: Deliver the runnable schedule and tally or a complete replay table, the shared vote ledger, and hearing and adoption counts.
shared: Give a fictional station committee four proposals for managing the found key, bench, bell, and service door. Compare two meeting agendas under one time cap.
sources: Le Matricule des Anges · Objets des délits

title: One animatic, three ways to see a beat
line: Retell six fixed beats by changing movement timing or what the frame lets the viewer see.
thesis: Translate Queneau’s repeated incident into animation by making each variation an observable operation on the same action. Let one cut suggest hesitation and another direct attention to incomplete evidence.
state: ◻(Incident) has six ordered events and protected facts. ◻(AssetSet) contains shared layers, poses, and sound. ◻(Animatic) has an exposure sheet and viewing rectangle. [retime] changes holds and transitions. [reframe] changes the visible field.
invariant: Lock the rigs or artwork, protected key poses, props, event order, sound bed, and 288-frame runtime at 24 fps. The timing variant changes holds and transitions while keeping the baseline frame. The framing variant keeps the baseline exposure sheet and uses one altered viewing rectangle.
concurrency: Freeze a playable baseline, then assign timing and framing to separate branches. Keep branch writes disjoint. Review each against the baseline before trying a combination.
swarm: Have one animator build the baseline and event anchors, another prepare exposure-sheet changes, and a framing editor control visibility. Let a viewer log the beats from the rendered clips.
proof: Render a baseline and two twelve-second animatics. In the timing variant lengthen anticipation before the envelope opens and pay back the frames elsewhere. In the framing variant limit peripheral visibility and give each protected action a cue within the smaller field.
fixture: Start with six windows of 48 frames. Give the timing branch window lengths 36, 36, 72, 48, 48, and 48. In the framing branch preserve the six original event windows and use one fixed crop chosen from the baseline stage. Count decoded frames and log concrete visual cues for E01–E06 in all three exports.
critic: Watch each clip once before consulting the cue map. Identify all six actions and the strongest perceived shift in expectation. Check that the crop preserves visible evidence and that the timing branch drew its evidence from the same poses.
inquiry: If the variants read alike, compare the actual added hold and what the crop conceals. Revise the operator’s range using the same baseline and evaluate the new render as a distinct run.
branch: Combine timing and framing in a fourth controlled export and compare both single-change runs. Check for a timing–visibility interaction at the opening cue.
deliver: Deliver three playable animatics, shared asset and pose IDs, the exposure sheets, the crop rectangle, and an event-by-event screening record.
shared: Hold on the closed envelope before E03 to change the visitor’s apparent intent. Try a restricted window centered on the handoff to the bench and make the door’s closure legible in all cuts.
sources: Bibliothèque nationale de France · Exercices de style
Documents Queneau’s work and an edition that gives its variations visual treatment.
Documents Matt Madden’s transfer of the repeated incident to the grammar of comics.
Documents a screen adaptation using text-to-video. The exposure-sheet and framing rules here define a separate SCION exercise.
